query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor dispersion of ZrC into the high‐entropy alloy (HEA) bond coat (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi) will improve its durability and reliability under high-temperature thermal barrier coating (TBC) service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: An untreated HEA bond coat (typically a CrMnFeCoNi alloy) prepared by conventional plasma transferred arc (PTA) deposition without any ceramic additive.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled addition (~4 wt%) of fine ZrC particles into the HEA feedstock during the PTA deposition process to form an in situ dispersion within the bond coat.
generation.conditions: The modified coating is to be evaluated under high-temperature cyclic exposures (e.g., thermal cycling between room temperature and ~1000 °C) in an oxidizing environment that simulates turbine operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The dispersion of ZrC as a second phase distributed within the predominantly FCC HEA matrix.
generation.mechanism: The ZrC particles are expected to act as stable, oxidation‐resistant barriers that inhibit inter-diffusion and the outward transport of reactive species. This second-phase dispersion refines the microstructure, strengthens the matrix via dispersion strengthening, and decreases the formation and propagation of damaging oxide scales or spallation during thermal cycling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated HEA bond coat, the ZrC-doped coating should exhibit reduced oxidation rates, improved adhesion, and lower spallation or cracking—resulting in a more durable and reliable bond coat under high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: The performance of the standard HEA bond coat without ZrC under similar high-temperature thermal cycling and oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected when the ZrC content is optimized (e.g., around 4 wt%); excessive additions might lead to phase segregation or embrittlement. Also, the improvement is anticipated primarily within the service temperature range typical for TBCs (approximately room temperature to 1000 °C) and may not extend to conditions outside this range.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies (e.g., on corrosion resistance improvements in similar HEA coatings) support the potential benefit of ZrC additions, the exact magnitude of improved durability under rapid thermal cycling and high oxidizing flux remains uncertain and may require further optimization of particle size and distribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bond coatings on identical substrates using the plasma transferred arc process: one set of standard CrMnFeCoNi HEA coatings (control) and a second set with an added 4 wt% ZrC. Subject both sets to accelerated thermal cycling in air (e.g., cycles between room temperature and 1000 °C with 1-hour dwell times at the high temperature for a total of 100 cycles).
measurements: Quantify oxidation scale thickness and composition using SEM/EDS and XRD before and after cycling.
Assess adhesion strength via standardized pull-off tests.
Evaluate spallation or cracking using optical and scanning electron microscopy.
Measure weight changes or mass losses as an indicator of oxidation and degradation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ZrC-enhanced HEA coatings do not show statistically significant improvements in oxidation resistance, adhesion strength, or reduced spallation/cracking compared to the unmodified controls under the defined test conditions, then the hypothesis that ZrC addition enhances coating durability and reliability would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ZrC can effectively improve the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating, and the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating increases with increasing ZrC content. The annual corrosion rate of the 04ZrC coating in a 1 mol/L NaCl solution is only 21.5% of that of the HEA. Consequently, the addition of ZrC to the FeCoCrNiMn high-entropy alloy coating holds promise for applications in corrosion resistance, particularly in oceanic environments.
